title: When Your Child Plans the Family Trip
text: Last February, Katrina was having trouble organising a family spring break trip, so she turned to an unconventional travel agent: Leo Kugel of Silver Spring, Md. Leo set aside the original Caribbean plan in favour of New Orleans, chose a hotel with something for everyone and tracked down an inexpensive flight. Leo is at least as tall as your average travel agent, but he is in fact my nephew. “We were stalled out,” Katrina told me. “And he said ‘I’ll take it from here.’ I was a little bit skeptical.” Apart from a tweak to the flight, though, everyone — Katrina, my brother Jeremy, my younger nephew Grady, my mom (a.k.a. Grammy) and my Aunt Nancy — went along with his choices, including a stay at Le Pavillon. When I heard about this, I may have tilted my head the way a dog does when it hears a weird noise. When did children suddenly pick up travel planning skills? I'm fairly sure the first time I chose a hotel was when I met my girlfriend in England at age 23. Actually, she probably chose it. But times have changed. “The general concept of your children influencing your vacation,” said Karen Cicero, travel editor at Parents magazine, “whether helping pick the destination or planning part of the trip, is a trend.” I'm skeptical when people use that word, but she pointed to a 2015 survey of 540 parents by YouGov for HomeAway, the vacation rental site, showing that millennial parents are more likely than older parents to let their children ages 6 to 18 pick a destination themselves. It makes sense. These days trip planning happens mostly online, and children know a thing or two about the internet.

title: Activists Hilariously Troll Chickenhawk Trump Right Behind The White House
text: Sharp-eyed CBS reporter Rebecca Shabad surely wasn't the first person to spot the giant inflatable chicken now on display behind the White House, but she was the first to tweet about it, on August 9, 2017: "BREAKING: There's an inflatable chicken with Trump's hair behind the White House." I don't know whether Ms. Shabad remembers that chicken, but it looks like it has been resurrected (reinflated?) from the props the Tax Day marchers used back in April. Writing for Slate, Danelle Morton described how the Trump Chickens came about after she found them for sale in China a month earlier: "A bit restless, I began Googling around for a symbol grotesque enough for our cause, something bloated that would block out the sky like a Macy's Thanksgiving Day balloon. I punched in TRUMP BALLOON into the search bar and discovered the Trump chicken: a huge inflatable rooster that bore an uncanny resemblance to Donald Trump. For China's Lunar New Year celebration, which kicked off the Year of the Rooster, inflatable versions of the Trump rooster could be found all over China. The Chinese, of course, aren't very happy with Trump, who taunted China on the campaign trail and flirted with Taiwan during the transition. The inflatable Trump Rooster Cock as a listing on Alibaba, China's equivalent of Amazon, calls it mocked his bluster with its swooping butterscotch pompadour and tiny hands shaped to mimic the way the president pinches his fingers. Some of the inflatables were gigantic, as tall as 60 feet. I couldn't believe what I'd found. In China this may be the Trump Rooster Cock, but in America it would be the Trump chicken." It was glorious. Welcome back, Trump Rooster Cock.

title: Roger Ailes Signals Possible Lawsuit Against New York Magazine
text: A lawyer representing Roger Ailes, the former chairman of Fox News, has sent New York magazine a letter suggesting that Mr. Ailes might take legal action over the magazine's reporting about him. Lauren Starke, a spokeswoman for the magazine, said Charles J. Harder, who represented Hulk Hogan in his successful lawsuit against Gawker Media, had contacted the magazine by email and asked it to preserve documents related to Mr. Ailes in preparation for a possible defamation claim. According to Ms. Starke, Mr. Harder sent the email on behalf of Mr. Ailes and his wife, Elizabeth. The Financial Times first reported the move. Mr. Harder did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Gabriel Sherman, a reporter at the magazine, has written extensively about Mr. Ailes and about the sexual harassment allegations by female employees that led to his ouster as chairman of Fox News in July. On Friday, New York published a lengthy article by Mr. Sherman about Mr. Ailes and his downfall, and in July Mr. Sherman was the first to report that Rupert Murdoch and his sons, Lachlan and James, had decided to remove Mr. Ailes from his post. Mr. Sherman declined to comment on Mr. Harder's request. The magazine said that Mr. Sherman's work "is and has been carefully reported." Mr. Harder, a Hollywood lawyer, has recently become a big name in media circles for taking on publications on behalf of his clients. In March he won a $140 million judgment for Hulk Hogan, the former professional wrestler whose real name is Terry G. Bollea, in a lawsuit against Gawker Media. That case was a professional breakout for Mr. Harder, who had previously been known for handling — and usually settling — more routine rights enforcement cases for celebrities.

title: Young Syrian Torchbearer Puts Spotlight on Brazil’s Welcome for Refugees
text: The Olympic torch relay certainly suffered its share of indignities this summer as it made its way across this vast country toward Rio de Janeiro. Government employees protesting over unpaid wages tried to disrupt its progress. Pranksters threw buckets of water in an attempt to put out the flame. In one particularly embarrassing episode, a soldier shot dead a jaguar — the official mascot of the Rio Games — after it escaped from its handlers during a ceremony in the Amazonian city of Manaus. Yet the antipathy that many Brazilians feel toward the Olympics briefly disappeared when onlookers cheered Hanan Dacka, a Syrian refugee, as she jogged through the nation's capital, Brasília, holding the Olympic flame. “Today I don’t feel like a refugee, but like any other Brazilian girl carrying the torch,” Hanan, who came to Brazil last year from a refugee camp in Jordan, told reporters during her leg of the relay in May. At a time when Europe and the United States have angrily debated calls to accept larger numbers of refugees, the choice of Hanan as a torchbearer has drawn attention to Brazil's role as a haven for Syrian asylum seekers. Brazil has taken in about 2,300 Syrian refugees, according to the National Committee for Refugees, a government agency. And with nearly 6,400 humanitarian visas issued to Syrians, officials say, the numbers are expected to climb significantly. Unlike in the United States, where the prospect of resettling Syrian refugees has become politically polarizing, in Brazil, also a nation of immigrants, the influx has been largely welcomed. Some three million Brazilians can trace their ancestry to Syrian migrants who started arriving at the beginning of the 20th century. It also helps that Brazil has been spared the Islamist extremist violence that has traumatized Europe and the United States.

title: Rumbling Bali volcano prompts travel warnings from Australia, Singapore
text: Fears of an imminent volcanic eruption on the holiday island of Bali led several countries to issue travel warnings, as Indonesian authorities hurried to evacuate tens of thousands of people living in the danger zone. Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, the United States and the U.K. issued advisories on Monday and over the weekend warning that heightened volcanic activity at Mount Agung in eastern Bali could disrupt flights to one of the world's most popular tourist destinations. "Given the possible eruption of Mount Agung, Singaporeans should defer non-essential travel to the affected areas at this juncture," the foreign ministry said in an online statement. Bali's international airport was operating as normal on Monday, as were tourist sites across the island. Indonesian authorities have set up a 12-km (7.5 miles) exclusion zone around the crater. On Monday the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) said some 62,000 people lived inside the danger zone around the volcano and that all of them had to evacuate, although only 50,000 had so far moved to the temporary shelters set up in neighboring villages. "There are some who are staying behind because the volcano hasn't erupted yet or because of religious beliefs," said BNPB spokesman Sutopo Purwo Nugroho. "Our staff are combing the area and urging everyone to evacuate," he said at a news conference in the Indonesian capital, Jakarta. Nugroho said Mount Agung had entered a "critical phase", meaning that magma has risen closer to the surface, as shown by hundreds of shallow volcanic tremors that have shaken the area in recent days. Evacuees are being housed in makeshift shelters such as town halls and school gyms. Host communities were supplying food and water, while the central and local governments were providing tents, blankets and other relief.

title: Arkansas Hurries to Execute 8 Men Within 10 Days
text: Next month the state of Arkansas plans to execute eight inmates over a period of 10 days, a pace of executions unmatched in recent American history and driven by the looming expiration date of a drug the state uses for lethal injections. The eight men facing execution — four black and four white — are among 34 death row inmates in Arkansas, where capital punishment has been on hold since 2005 because of legal challenges and difficulty obtaining the drugs for lethal injections. All eight were convicted of murders committed between 1989 and 1999, and supporters of the death penalty and of victims' rights in the state have been frustrated that the cases have dragged on for so long. At a news conference this week, Gov. Asa Hutchinson, a Republican and former federal prosecutor, appeared to regret that the executions were stacked so closely together. “I would love to have those extended over a period of multiple months and years, but that’s not the circumstances that I find myself in,” said Mr. Hutchinson, who took office in 2015. “And, again, the families of the victims that have endured this for so many years deserve a conclusion to it.” In a statement on Friday, Mr. Hutchinson said the executions had to be scheduled close together because of doubts over the future availability of one of the three drugs the state uses in its procedure. State officials have said before that the expiration date for Arkansas's supply of midazolam would pass in April. The drug has been used in several botched and gruesome lethal injections in other states in recent years. Amid the controversy over such cases, a number of pharmaceutical companies have barred their drugs from being used for capital punishment.

title: Merkel allies worry about former East Germany's shift to the right
text: The premiers of two regions where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party made big gains in Sunday's national election warned that Chancellor Angela Merkel's conservatives must change course to halt the former East Germany's drift to the right. Merkel's Christian Democrats (CDU) suffered heavy losses across much of Germany in the election, in which the anti-immigration AfD became the first far-right party to enter the national parliament in over half a century. The calls for a shift to the right add to the challenge Merkel faces as she tries to put together an already tricky three-party coalition with the left-wing Greens, the pro-business Free Democrats (FDP) and her own increasingly fractious party. The prospects for a three-way pact nonetheless improved on Saturday, when the Greens voted at a special congress to begin exploratory talks on a deal despite reservations about the harder-line immigration policies of the other parties. The AfD's surge set off soul-searching in the conservative camp, with many blaming it on Merkel's 2015 decision to open the doors to over a million migrants fleeing war and poverty in the Middle East and Africa. The conservative premiers of Saxony, where the AfD came first, and of Saxony Anhalt urged the CDU to move to the right to stem its losses. "People want Germany to stay Germany," Stanislaw Tillich, premier of Saxony, said in an interview with the Funke newspaper network. "They don't want parallel societies and rising criminality." Rainer Haseloff, premier of Saxony-Anhalt, echoed him, telling the newspaper Die Welt: "People want to know how Germany will preserve its identity." These calls bring the two influential state leaders closer to the CDU's Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), which wants a hard ceiling on immigration.

title: 5 takeaways from the first presidential debate
text: Inside Hofstra University there were a couple of not-so-subtle signs that Donald Trump had lost Monday night's much-anticipated debate against Hillary Clinton, and lost it badly. The first was the audible groaning from some of his supporters inside the debate hall (caught by my attentive colleague Steve Shepard) as Trump wandered defensively through one answer after another against a very focused, very energized and very well-rehearsed Hillary Clinton. Another tell: once the 90-minute sparring match was over, Clinton's team all but bounded into the spin room – more in glassy-eyed disbelief than in visible elation that things had gone so much better than expected. The GOP nominee's people, by contrast, trickled into the media pen like surly seventh-graders heading to homeroom the day before summer vacation. “F—k, let’s do this,” a prominent Trump surrogate said before plunging into a scrum. Trump and his new-ish messaging team have worked hard to turn the avatar of populist rage into a reasonable facsimile of someone you could picture sitting in the Oval Office. But that best-laid plan came apart on Monday – amid Clinton's steely assault and the dignified questioning of NBC's Lester Holt, who struck a deft balance between facilitator, BS detector and lion tamer. Within minutes of the opening bell, Clinton's attacks had pushed a domesticated Donald to go feral – he bellowed, interrupted her again and again, grunted, and toward the bedraggled end turned muted and pouty. “It was bizarre,” said David Plouffe, Barack Obama's campaign manager, who, like many Clinton allies, looked visibly relieved. “He was clearly rattled, and clearly focused on defending himself, which I’m told narcissists are prone to do, and he clearly faded at the end. It’s not like she’s going to jump out to a 10-point lead, but this was good.”
